Release notes
Sourced from urllib3's releases.

2.8.0
🚀 urllib3 is fundraising for HTTP/2 support
urllib3 is raising ~$40,000 USD to release HTTP/2 support and ensure long-term sustainable maintenance of the project. If your company or organization uses Python and would benefit from HTTP/2 support in Requests, pip, cloud SDKs, and thousands of other projects please consider contributing financially to ensure HTTP/2 support is developed sustainably and maintained for the long-haul.
Thank you for your support.
Security
Fixed the following security issues:

The TLS configuration for HTTPS proxies could be ignored or overridden. (High severity, GHSA-8988-9cw3-xx77)
HTTPResponse.stream() and read_chunked() could buffer a chunk-size line of unbounded length in memory. (High severity, GHSA-vxq7-64xx-v4gw)
Chunked Deflate streaming could enter an infinite loop. (Medium severity, GHSA-gh4c-6fx4-qh6g)

[!IMPORTANT]
urllib3 2.8.0 fixes HTTPS proxy TLS configuration being ignored or overridden by destination settings. Configurations relying on that behavior may require changes.
Configure proxy CA certificates and client certificates in proxy_ssl_context, and proxy identity checks with proxy_assert_hostname or proxy_assert_fingerprint. Destination client certificates and identity overrides no longer apply to HTTPS forwarding proxy connections.

[!NOTE]
CVE IDs had not yet been assigned to these advisories at the time of release due to a backlog at GitHub's CNA.

Deprecations & Removals

Deprecated using an empty collection as the Retry option allowed_methods to retry any verb. (#5044)

Features

Added Url.auth_decoded and Url.auth_decoded_joined convenience properties to the result of parse_url(). (#4945)
Added basic_auth_encoding and proxy_basic_auth_encoding parameters to urllib3.util.make_headers(). (#5092)

Bugfixes

Fixed response header handling to replace obsolete folded header lines (obs-fold) with spaces in accordance with RFC 9112, preventing raw CRLF sequences from appearing in header values such as Set-Cookie. (#1362)

Fixed usage of proxy_ssl_context with ProxyManager when use_forwarding_for_https=True. Passing ssl_context instead of proxy_ssl_context for HTTPS proxies in this configuration now emits a FutureWarning and will raise an error in v3.0. (#2577)

Changed behavior of the default ConnectionPool.pool initialization. LifoQueue is now resolved from the queue module after the ConnectionPool is instantiated instead of using the default cached QueueCls class property. This is done because sometimes the queue.LifoQueue is monkey-patched late in the program, such as by gevent. (#3289)

Raised UnrewindableBodyError instead of ValueError when retrying a request whose body had tell() but not seek(). (#3779)

Decoded percent-encoded SOCKS proxy credentials before authenticating with the proxy server. (#3785)

Fixed HTTPResponse.drain_conn() to discard unread response data in 64 KiB chunks (same as the default amt when doing HTTPResponse.stream(...)). (#5019)

Fixed is_ipaddress() to detect non-standard IPv4 forms accepted by socket.connect, such as hex (0x7f000001), octal (0177.0.0.1), and decimal integers (2130706433), ensuring SSL certificate verification uses the correct mode for these addresses. (#5029)

Fixed HTTPConnectionPool.urlopen raising a misleading FullPoolError instead of ValueError when called with an invalid timeout argument on a pool created with block=True. (#5059)

Fixed port-zero handling to preserve explicit :0 values instead of substituting the default ports 80 or 443 in URL parsing, pool selection, proxy configuration, connection_from_url(), and HTTP/2 request authority. (#5071, #5101)

Fixed a bug where PoolManager passed the assert_hostname and assert_fingerprint parameters to HTTP connection pools. (#5077)

Fixed HTTPConnectionPool.urlopen() and HTTP proxy forwarding to strip URL fragments from absolute request targets before sending requests. (#5079)

Rationale for this change
Iceberg Java sends the DeleteObjects body to the S3 signing service, as the REST spec says to. PyIceberg doesn't. The body is the only place the keys being deleted appear, so REST catalogs like Lakekeeper reject DeleteObjects sign requests without it.
Since FsspecFileIO.delete sends DeleteObjects even for a single file, PyIceberg can't delete files through remote signing with these catalogs today.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. A new s3 test writes, reads, and deletes a file through S3V4RestSigner against the S3 container that the integration-test-s3 CI job runs. A requests_mock signing endpoint SigV4-signs each request with the container's credentials. The test checks that only the DeleteObjects sign request carries a body, and it fails without the fix.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Sign requests for DeleteObjects now include the request body.
AI Disclosure: This PR was authored by Claude Code (Opus 5.5) but directed and overseen by me.

Bumps gcsfs from 2026.6.0 to 2026.8.1.

Release notes
Sourced from gcsfs's releases.

2026.8.1
What's Changed
Bug Fixes
Fixes fsspec/gcsfs#1048: In release 2026.8.0, cat_file began using a default concurrency of 4 instead of 1. This caused a performance regression for small cat_file operations with unknown sizes, as an unnecessary _info() request was being triggered to determine the size for concurrent reads.
Full Changelog: fsspec/[email removed]...2026.8.1
2026.8.0
What's Changed
Adaptive Concurrent Prefetching is now the default read path
Enhanced read path via adaptive concurrent prefetching is now the default  in GCSFS.
Starting with this version, GCSFS predicts the next byte range an application will read, fetches it in the background across several concurrent HTTP requests, and keeps the bytes in memory before next read() is called. Network round-trips overlap with application compute instead of blocking calls where compute has to wait for data to be fetched. We are also enabling read concurrency, so a single reader is no longer limited by the bandwidth of a single HTTP connection.
GCSFS prefetcher adapts to workload read IO patterns. It tracks the rolling average of recent read sizes and scales the prefetch window linearly with the detected sequential streak, rather than using a fixed block size or exponential doubling. This is inline to what modern Linux kernels will do to balance prefetch and memory footprint. When the pattern turns random read i.e. we are not able to leverage the prefetched buffer to answer the next read() call, it drains the buffer to zero, so that random-access workloads pay no bandwidth or memory penalty.
Why this matters for AI/ML workloads

Model loading and checkpoint restore are typically large sequential reads - and prefetcher shines there. In our benchmarking, a single-stream sequential throughput improved from 23.69 MB/s to 658.71 MB/s for 1 MB I/O, and from 156 MB/s to 736 MB/s for 16 MB I/O.
Training data pipelines stay fed. Parquet and sharded dataset reads issue small-to-medium sequential ranges that previously suffered from low throughput, but now achieve significantly more; at 16 MB I/O throughput rises from 150 MB/s to 730 MB/s. Reducing the wait time for data loading improves accelerator goodput(amount of time accelerator is utilised for training than waiting).
Multi-worker dataloader scaling. The prefetcher manufactures its own parallelism per worker instead of relying on process count alone.

def eval(self, manifest: ManifestFile) -> bool:
    if partitions := manifest.partitions:
        self.partition_fields = partitions      # shared by every thread
        return visit(self.partition_filter, self)
If one thread stores manifest A's summaries and another stores manifest B's before A reads its first predicate leaf, A is judged by B's partition bounds. When A holds the files being deleted it is skipped, _validate_required_deletes never finds them, and the overwrite fails with ValidationException: Missing required files to delete even though the files are live. The reporter measures roughly 1 in 700 overwrites on production tables with many manifests, each one discarding the commit and its work.
The opposite direction — keeping a manifest that should have been skipped — is harmless, because the entry comparison finds nothing in it.
The fix
Evaluate on a shallow copy, so the bound filter stays shared and read-only while each call gets its own summaries. This is the first of the three options @QlikFrederic suggested, and it leaves the hot path allocating one small object per manifest rather than rebinding the filter.
As far as I can see _deleted_entries is the only caller that shares an evaluator across threads — DataScan.plan_files, _existing_manifests and _DeleteFiles evaluate one manifest at a time — but the fix belongs in eval either way, since the object is reachable from the factory and nothing about its contract says single-threaded.
The test
test_manifest_evaluator_judges_each_manifest_by_its_own_summaries forces the interleaving deterministically rather than racing: it holds the thread evaluating the in-range manifest at its first predicate leaf, after the summaries are stored, until a second thread has evaluated an out-of-range manifest. No sleeps, and it uses the ThreadPoolExecutor/Event idiom already present in this test module.
It fails on main with assert False on "manifest holds id == INT_MIN_VALUE and must be read" and passes with the fix.
Verification
Run locally against tests/expressions/test_visitors.py:

new test with the fix: 1 passed
new test with the fix reverted: 1 failed, on the intended assertion
whole module, fix applied: 73 passed
whole module on unmodified main: 72 passed

I could not run the full suite locally because tests/conftest.py imports moto, which I could not install in this environment, so those runs used --noconftest; that accounts for 19 identical fixture-lookup errors in both the before and after runs, and it is why the counts differ by exactly the one added test. CI will cover the rest.
title: fix(expressions): stop a shared manifest evaluator from mixing up manifests

body:
Closes #3833
Rationale for this change
ArrowProjectionVisitor.list rebuilds a list whose element is a struct with pa.LargeListArray.from_arrays(list_array.offsets, value_array). The offsets alone cannot express a null list, so every null list<struct<...>> came out as an empty list. The visitor runs on both the read and the write path; on write the empty list is persisted into the Parquet file, so the null is gone for every reader, not only for pyiceberg.
Reproduction from the issue (pyarrow 25.0.1):
l_struct  in=[[{'x': 1}], [], None, [{'x': 3}]]  out=[[{'x': 1}], [], [], [{'x': 3}]]
l_int     in=[[1], [], None, [3]]                out=[[1], [], None, [3]]

This PR rebuilds the list with pa.Array.from_buffers, reusing the validity and offsets buffers (and the array offset) of the original list and swapping in the projected element array. Passing mask=list_array.is_null() to from_arrays would fix the unsliced case, but Arrow rejects a mask together with sliced offsets (Null bitmap with offsets slice not supported) for LargeListArray, so sliced batches would start raising. Reusing the buffers keeps the array offset and avoids that.
The integration test test_null_list_and_map asserted the corrupted value with the correct assertion commented out; the correct assertion is restored.
Are these changes tested?

New unit test test__to_requested_schema_null_list_of_structs in tests/io/test_pyarrow.py, parametrized over pa.list_ and pa.large_list, covering a full batch and a sliced one. It fails on main (At index 2 diff: [] != None) and passes with this change.
Restored the real assertion in tests/integration/test_reads.py::test_null_list_and_map.
make test and make lint pass locally.

Are there any user-facing changes?
Null lists of structs are now preserved on read and write instead of being turned into empty lists.

body:
Closes #4069
Rationale for this change
PyArrowFileIO.__init__ caches filesystems with lru_cache(self._initialize_fs). The cache wraps a bound method, which holds a strong reference back to self. Since self also holds the cache, every PyArrowFileIO is part of a reference cycle.
So when the last user reference to a FileIO goes away, refcounting can't free it. The FileIO and every filesystem it cached stay alive until Python's cycle collector happens to run, along with their open connections and connection pools (S3, GCS, ADLS, ...). In long-running processes that create many catalogs or tables, this shows up as connections and memory that pile up for no visible reason.
This PR replaces the bound-method cache with a small module-level factory, _fs_by_scheme_cache(file_io). It returns an lru_cache-wrapped closure that holds only a weakref to the FileIO. That removes the cycle, so the FileIO and its cached filesystems are freed by plain refcounting as soon as they're unused.

fs_by_scheme still behaves exactly as before: same signature, same caching, and cache_info() still works.
__getstate__ is unchanged. __setstate__ rebuilds the cache through the same factory, so unpickled instances don't have the cycle either.
Tests that patch PyArrowFileIO._initialize_fs on the class keep working, because the closure calls it through the instance.

Out of scope, possible follow-ups:

FsspecFileIO may have the same pattern.
SqlCatalog creates a second FileIO, which is worth checking separately.

Are these changes tested?
Yes. Two new tests in tests/io/test_pyarrow.py:

test_pyarrow_file_io_freed_by_refcounting: turns off the cycle collector (gc.disable(), restored afterwards), creates a FileIO, fills the cache with fs_by_scheme("file", None), drops the FileIO, and checks that a weakref to it is now dead.
test_pyarrow_file_io_pickle_round_trip_keeps_cache_and_refcounting: pickles and unpickles a FileIO, checks the restored copy still resolves a LocalFileSystem and caches it, and checks it's also freed by refcounting alone.

Both tests fail on main and pass with this change. The existing test_pyarrow_file_io_fs_by_scheme_cache test, which uses cache_info(), still passes. make test passes (4255 passed, 5 skipped), and make lint passes.
Are there any user-facing changes?
No API changes. The only difference users will see is that a PyArrowFileIO and its filesystems (with their connections) are released as soon as nothing references them, instead of waiting for the cycle collector.
title: fix(io): break PyArrowFileIO reference cycle so filesystems are freed by refcounting

body:
Rationale for this change
The spec's Column Projection rules say that when a field isn't present in a data file, we resolve its value in order:

the identity partition value from the manifest's partition struct, if present
the column found via schema.name-mapping.default
the field's initial-default
null

Today _get_column_projection_values only records the identity partition value when it's non-null. So when a file's partition value is null, we skip rule 1 and fall through to rule 3, as if the partition metadata had nothing to say. This was harmless before v3 because initial-default was always null anyway, but with a non-null initial-default we now read the default instead of null.
This came up while reviewing #4082, which this builds on to also handle partition columns used only in the row filter.
Are these changes tested?
Yes
Are there any user-facing changes?
Only for v3 tables with a non-null initial-default on an identity-partitioned column on null partition. This is a bug fix that conforms to the spec: https://iceberg.apache.org/spec/#column-projection

Rationale for this change
The remove_statistics() method on the statistics update builder is dropping updates which are queued before it.
This PR supersedes #3557
table.update_statistics() \
    .set_statistics(statistics_file) \
    .remove_statistics(other_snapshot_id) \
    .commit()
When remove_statistics() is called, the update queued by set_statistics() gets dropped, so at commit, only the remove is preserved. The side effects of this could be that the query engines plan with stale statistics.
This happens as = is used in remove_statistics() method. = replaces the builder's list of pending updates instead of appending to it. set_statistics() is using +=.
The fix is to use += in remove_statistics() method, like in set_statistics().

The test sets a new statistics file for s2, then removes s1's statistics.
After the commit, s2 points to the new file and s1 has no statistics. Both changes are applied.
On the main branch, this test fails, the set_statistics() for s2 gets dropped, s2 keeps pointing to its old file.
With the fix, make test, 4,254 passed, and make lint passing.
Are there any user-facing changes?
No API changes. set-then-remove now applies both updates.

Rationale for this change
_StrictMetricsEvaluator raises when a predicate references a nested column, so delete() and overwrite() with such a filter fail during planning:
schema = pa.schema([pa.field("id", pa.int64()), pa.field("s", pa.struct([pa.field("x", pa.int64())]))])

tbl.append(pa.table({"id": [1, 2], "s": [{"x": 1}, {"x": 5}]}, schema=schema))
tbl.delete("s.x != 5")
# ValueError: Cannot find field, might be nested or missing: 3
NotEqualTo, In and NotIn look up the field in the top-level struct before checking bounds, so they fail even on files that pyiceberg writes itself, which have no nested bounds. The range and equality predicates fail once the file has bounds for the nested column, for example files written by Spark. Java fixed this in apache/iceberg#11261: for a nested column, strict evaluation returns ROWS_MIGHT_NOT_MATCH because nested null counts are not reliable. This change does the same. It also matters for #3810, which starts writing nested bounds from pyiceberg. After it, the delete above rewrites the file and leaves [{'id': 2, 's': {'x': 5}}].
Are these changes tested?
Yes. test_strict_nested_column in tests/expressions/test_evaluator.py covers nested columns with and without bounds, and it fails on main with the ValueError above. The evaluator, visitor and residual tests pass.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes. delete() and overwrite() with a filter on a nested struct field no longer raise.
Written with help from Claude.

body:
Closes #3621 (part of #1551). Stacked on #3624, which adds ManifestListWriterV3. Only the last commit belongs to this PR; I will rebase once #3624 merges.
Rationale for this change
Every commit to a V3 table fails on a REST catalog. _SnapshotProducer._commit sets first-row-id on the new snapshot but never sets added-rows, and the spec requires both together. The REST fixture rejects the snapshot:
java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Invalid added-rows (required when first-row-id is set): null

Without a server check, the table metadata goes wrong instead. add_snapshot computes next-row-id from added-rows, so next-row-id becomes None after the first commit and the next commit fails.
This PR sets added-rows to writer.next_row_id - first_row_id, which is the number of row IDs ManifestListWriterV3 assigned. Java's SnapshotProducer computes it the same way. The count includes existing rows in manifests that had no first_row_id, so next-row-id always moves past every assigned ID.
It also removes _calculate_added_rows. Nothing called it, and it counted only added_rows_count from the snapshot's own manifests, which would undercount the rows that the writer assigns.
Out of scope: a V3 table created by new_table_metadata has next-row-id = None, so a commit to it still fails. A REST server sets it to 0 on create, which hides this. That belongs with writing V3 metadata (#3551).
Rewritten manifests do not keep row IDs on EXISTING entries yet, so a merge append or partial delete moves them. #3972 fixes this by inheriting first_row_id on read. added-rows already matches Java in both cases.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. Three new tests in tests/table/test_snapshots.py commit to an empty V3 table inside a transaction, because writing a V3 metadata.json is not supported yet:

two appends: (first_row_id, added_rows) is (0, 3), then (3, 3), and next-row-id is 6
add_files: (0, 3), next-row-id is 3
a delete that rewrites a data file: the 2 surviving rows get new IDs, (3, 2), and next-row-id is 5

All three fail without the change. The unit suite passes locally.
This PR also un-skips the integration test test_v3_write_and_read_row_lineage. It now appends twice and reads _row_id and _last_updated_sequence_number with Spark (Iceberg 1.11.0), which must see row IDs 0 to 5 with sequence numbers 1 and 2. It passes with the change and fails without it on the same Invalid added-rows error.

t.add_files([f"file://{src}"])           # 3 rows
cat.load_table(ident).append(data)        # 3 rows
cat.load_table(ident).delete("id == 1")   # rewrites both files
Before, on #3624 (c152089d):
lineage.t_2890d52f format-version=3 next-row-id=0
CommitStateUnknownException: RESTError 500: ... Invalid added-rows (required when first-row-id is set): null

After:

body:
Rationale for this change
Filters on float columns can miss rows, and delete() can delete the wrong rows:
import pyarrow as pa

from pyiceberg.catalog.memory import InMemoryCatalog
from pyiceberg.schema import Schema
from pyiceberg.types import FloatType, IntegerType, NestedField

catalog = InMemoryCatalog("default")
catalog.create_namespace("default")
schema = Schema(NestedField(1, "id", IntegerType()), NestedField(2, "value", FloatType()))
tbl = catalog.create_table("default.t", schema=schema)
tbl.append(pa.table({"id": pa.array([1, 2, 3], pa.int32()), "value": pa.array([0.1, 0.4, 0.7], pa.float32())}))

print(tbl.scan(row_filter="value = 0.1").to_arrow()["id"].to_pylist())  # main: [], expected: [1]
tbl.delete("value != 0.1")
print(tbl.scan().to_arrow()["id"].to_pylist())  # main: [], expected: [1]
Why. A float column stores 32-bit values, and 0.1 as a 32-bit float is 0.10000000149011612. PyIceberg keeps the filter value as the 64-bit 0.1. To decide which files to read, it compares the filter value with each file's min and max (or with the partition value). These two numbers are not equal, so the file with 0.1 is skipped. Reading rows inside a file is fine, because the row filter turns the value into a 32-bit Arrow scalar (_convert_scalar). So the bug shows up when the value is a file's min or max, or a partition value.
Deletes use the same min/max check. For delete("value != 0.1"), PyIceberg decides that no row in the file is 0.1 and drops the whole file.
Data [0.1, 0.4, 0.7] in one file:

main
this PR

value = 0.1
[]
[1]

value <= 0.1
[]
[1]

value >= 0.7
[]
[3]

delete("value != 0.1"), then scan
[]
[1]

delete("value = 0.1"), then scan
[1, 2, 3]
[2, 3]

Fix. Convert the value to 32 bits when the float literal is created, in FloatLiteral.__init__. The spec defines float as a 32-bit IEEE 754 value (spec.md#L281). Java does the same: binding a double literal to a float column creates new FloatLiteral(value().floatValue()) (Literals.java#L380). This also removes _value32, which is now the same as .value.
A float initial-default read from table metadata is converted too, like Java (SingleValueParser.java#L79). Otherwise a filter on a column that is missing from older files would stop matching its default.
Reproduced on 0.12.0 and main.
Are these changes tested?
Yes.

tests/catalog/test_catalog_behaviors.py: new scan and delete tests on a float column, with and without an identity partition, for each catalog fixture. All 18 fail on main and pass with this change.
tests/expressions/test_literals.py::test_double_to_float_within_bound expected the old 64-bit value. It now expects the 32-bit value of 34.56 (34.560001373291016).
tests/expressions/test_visitors.py: new test for a missing float column with initial_default=0.1. It fails if only the filter value is converted.
tests/test_conversions.py::test_json_float_is_read_as_float32: a float default read from JSON (22.27) now comes back as its float32 value, while a double stays 22.27. It fails on main.
Unit tests on Linux (Python 3.11, with pyiceberg-core), after rebasing on current main (4ba3ba4): 4351 passed, 4331 on main. The difference is the 20 tests above that fail on main. 12 other failures are the same on both, from optional packages I don't have (Kerberos, Azure). My setup has no Cython Avro decoder, so tests/avro was not collected, and I ignored the pure-Python fallback warning on both sides. I couldn't run the Docker integration tests locally, so I rely on CI for them.
tests/integration/test_rest_schema.py::test_initial_default_all_columns: the float case set a default of 22.27, which is not exact in float32 and now reads back as 22.270000457763672 (CI caught this). It now uses 22.25, which is exact. The double case still uses 22.27.
prek run --files on the changed files passes.

Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes. Filters and deletes on float columns now return and remove the right rows. double columns are not affected.

body:
Rationale for this change
If you stop partitioning by a column and then drop that column, the next delete() breaks the table. The commit succeeds, but after that neither PyIceberg nor Spark can read the table.
import pyarrow as pa

from pyiceberg.catalog.memory import InMemoryCatalog

catalog = InMemoryCatalog("default")
catalog.create_namespace("default")
data = pa.Table.from_pydict({"id": [1, 2], "category": ["a", "b"]})
tbl = catalog.create_table("default.t", schema=data.schema)
with tbl.update_spec() as update:
    update.add_identity("category")
tbl.append(data)

with tbl.update_spec() as update:
    update.remove_field("category")   # 1. stop partitioning by category
with tbl.update_schema() as update:
    update.delete_column("category")  # 2. drop the column

tbl.delete("id == 1")                 # 3. commits fine
tbl.scan().to_arrow()                 # main: IndexError, expected: id = [2]
What goes wrong

The old partition spec still has a category field, but the column is gone, so its type becomes unknown.
When step 3 rewrites the manifest, unknown maps to Avro "null", so the optional field becomes the union ["null", "null"], which Avro does not allow. Reading that manifest back fails: IndexError in PyIceberg, Duplicate in union:null in Spark.

When it started

Before #3899 (including the 0.12.0 release): step 3 raises an error. The delete fails, but the table is untouched and still readable.
After #3899 (merged to main, not released yet): step 3 succeeds but writes a broken manifest, so the whole table becomes unreadable.

Fix
The spec says unknown is not stored in data files, and its Avro mapping is "null or omitted". This PR omits it:

Write (ManifestWriter._with_partition): unknown partition fields are left out of the manifest's Avro schema. The in-memory partition record keeps all fields, and the Avro writer already matches file fields to record positions by field ID, so nothing else changes on the write path.
Read (fetch_manifest_entry): today the partition tuple is read with only the fields in the file. If category is omitted from a (category, region) spec, the tuple comes back as Record('y') instead of Record(None, 'y'), so reading region at index 1 fails with IndexError (or reads a later field's value if more fields follow). The reader now takes the field list from the partition-spec in the manifest header and adds any omitted field back as an optional field, which reads as None. Manifests without omitted fields are read exactly as before. To do this, AvroFile now also accepts a function that builds the read schema from the file header.
Java passes the table's partition specs (specsById) into its manifest reader. Reading the spec from the header is its fallback, which Java marks as deprecated (ManifestReader.java#L156-L164). fetch_manifest_entry has no spec argument and has 12 call sites, so this PR reads the header and leaves the signature unchanged. Passing specs in could be a follow-up if preferred.

Reports from users

apache/iceberg#14343: same steps in Java (remove partition field, drop the column, then delete). Fixed in apache/iceberg#14356.
apache/iceberg#10234: Spark users also had their tables break after dropping an old partition column (an older, different error).

Are these changes tested?
Yes.

New tests (14 cases across catalogs and v1/v2; 13 fail on main and pass here, and 1 is a regression test that already passes on main):

tests/catalog/test_catalog_behaviors.py::test_delete_after_dropping_old_partition_source_column: the example above (v1 and v2, every catalog fixture), and the omitted field reads back as None.
tests/catalog/test_catalog_behaviors.py::test_filter_after_dropping_earlier_partition_source_column: partitioned by category and region, category dropped. Filtering on region returns the right rows after the first delete, and again after a second delete that reads and rewrites the same manifest.
tests/utils/test_manifest.py::test_write_manifest_skips_unknown_partition_field: the un […]

body:
Closes #4116
Rationale for this change
As described in the issue, an Avro named type (decimal_P_S, fixed_L, uuid_fixed) may only be defined once per schema; later uses must refer to it by name. PyIceberg couldn't read the reference form (TypeError: Type not recognized: decimal_10_2), so it failed on manifests written by Java and iceberg-rust, and it wrote the same definition every time a type was reused, which strict readers reject.

Read: AvroSchemaConversion remembers each named type (record, enum, fixed) it converts, and resolves a later string type with that name to the same Iceberg type. A repeated full definition is still accepted, so existing manifests keep working. The map is reset at the start of avro_to_iceberg.
Write: following the review, ConvertSchemaToAvro adds the field-id of the field, list element or map key/value that uses a fixed, decimal or uuid type to its name (decimal_10_2_1, fixed_3_5, uuid_fixed_7), the same way records are named r<field-id>. Field-ids are unique, so every definition has its own name and no bookkeeping of defined names is needed.

Are these changes tested?
Yes, in the existing test files:

tests/utils/test_schema_conversion.py: reading the reference form (the repro from the issue, plus fixed_3 and uuid_fixed), reading the repeated form, an unknown name still raising TypeError, and writing a schema with repeated decimal, fixed (one inside a struct) and uuid types, including a list element and a map key and value: each gets the field-id in its name and the result reads back to the same schema.
tests/avro/test_file.py: test_repeated_named_types_round_trip writes a file with two decimal(10,2) and two uuid fields through AvroOutputFile and reads it back with PyIceberg and with fastavro. Without the change, fastavro refuses the file with a SchemaParseException for the redefined name.

The new tests fail without the change. tests/utils/test_schema_conversion.py, tests/avro, tests/test_avro_sanitization.py and tests/utils/test_manifest.py pass. Failures in my environment from optional extras I didn't install are the same before and after the change. ruff 0.14.3 and mypy 1.18.2 (the pre-commit versions) are clean.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Manifests and manifest lists that refer to a named type by name can now be read, and the fixed, decimal and uuid types PyIceberg writes now have the field-id in their name.
I used an AI assistant to help draft parts of the code and tests; I reviewed the changes and ran the tests myself.

body:
Closes #4095
Rationale for this change
The REST spec's POST /v1/{prefix}/transactions/commit applies changes to several tables in one atomic operation, and the Java client exposes it as RESTCatalog.commitTransaction(...). PyIceberg had no way to call it, so write-audit-publish across tables or a backfill of related tables couldn't be published atomically from Python.
This adds Catalog.commit_transactions(*transactions):
orders_tx = orders.transaction()
orders_tx.append(new_orders)
items_tx = items.transaction()
items_tx.append(new_items)

catalog.commit_transactions(orders_tx, items_tx)  # both tables, or neither
What it does

REST catalog: sends each transaction's requirements and updates as one CommitTransactionRequest, adding the same AssertTableUUID that commit_transaction adds. The endpoint returns 204, so each table is refreshed afterwards and the transactions are cleared.
Other catalogs: the base Catalog raises NotImplementedError, so they can add support later.
Errors map like commit_table: 409 → CommitFailedException, 404 → NoSuchTableError, 500/502/504 → CommitStateUnknownException.
Files: on a definite failure (409, 404) the files written for the transactions are deleted. On an unknown outcome they're kept, because the catalog may already reference them. That's the same rule commit_transaction follows. A failed transaction can't be reused.
Rejected before anything is sent: no transactions, the same transaction twice, two transactions on one table, a transaction from another catalog, and CreateTableTransaction. Transactions without staged changes are skipped, and a call with only empty ones sends nothing. The exception is a snapshot operation that staged nothing, such as a delete whose filter matched no rows: it is sent with assert-ref-snapshot-id on its starting snapshot and no updates, so a concurrent change to that table fails the whole commit. commit_transaction validates the same case on the client; here the catalog checks it atomically with the other tables (the same requirement-only pattern as apache/polaris#5807).
Endpoint check: uses the server's advertised endpoints. For servers that don't list endpoints, transactions/commit is assumed supported, as in the Java client's DEFAULT_ENDPOINTS.

Not in this PR (open questions)

No retry on conflict. A 409 doesn't say which table conflicted, and replaying snapshot producers across tables is a bigger design. The caller re-stages and commits again, as with the Java client. Happy to follow up if you'd like retries.
Creating tables in a multi-table commit (with assert-create) could come later.
Entry point: I went with Catalog.commit_transactions(*transactions) as proposed in #4095. Glad to change it, for example to a context manager.

Are these changes tested?

tests/catalog/test_rest.py: 13 tests with a mocked server. They cover the request body, the prefix, each error status, file cleanup only when nothing was applied, skipping empty transactions, the requirement sent for a delete that matched nothing, the input checks and an unsupported endpoint.
tests/catalog/test_base.py: the base catalog raises NotImplementedError.

two tables each get a real append (and a property change) in one call, and both have the rows afterwards;
another writer appends to one table after the transactions were staged: the commit fails with CommitFailedException, and neither table gets the staged rows.

make test: 4273 passed. make lint passes on the changed files.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes: the new Catalog.commit_transactions method, and a "Multi-table commits" section in mkdocs/docs/api.md.

body:
Closes #4130
Rationale for this change
Parquet statistics do not track NaN values, so data files written by PyIceberg never carry nan_value_counts. The strict metrics evaluator reads a missing NaN count as "no NaN values" (as Java does, since Java's Parquet writers always record these counts). That means Table.delete("x < 5.0") drops a file containing [1.0, NaN] as a whole, so the NaN row is lost even though it does not match the filter.
This change counts NaN values of float and double columns in ParquetFormatWriter.write, including nested struct fields, list elements and map values. body:
Closes #4145.
Rationale for this change
PyArrowFileIO writes local (file://) files through pyarrow.fs.LocalFileSystem, whose output stream never calls fsync. The catalog then commits a pointer to the new metadata.json, so after a power loss the pointer can survive while the files it references are empty, and the table no longer loads. #4145 has the full trace and a power-cut reproduction.
This change makes a local write durable when its stream is closed, which is before any catalog commit can reference it:

PyArrowLocalFileSystem.open_output_stream now returns _SyncOnCloseOutputStream, a pyarrow.BufferedOutputStream over a pyarrow.OSFile. On close() it flushes, fsyncs the file, and then fsyncs the parent directory so that the new entry is durable too.
When open_output_stream has to create parent directories (for example metadata/ or data/ on the first write), it also fsyncs the parent of each directory it created.

The stream stays a native pyarrow stream with the same buffer size, so the Parquet, Avro and metadata writers are unchanged. Every caller already closes its stream explicitly or through with.
Scope, kept deliberately narrow:

Only PyArrowFileIO's local file system changes. FsspecFileIO's local file system has the same gap and could follow separately.
The SQLite catalog's own rollback-journal behaviour, which #4145 also mentions, is not touched.
On Windows, directories cannot be opened, so only the file is synced there.
If a caller passes compression or metadata to open_output_stream, it still gets pyarrow's own stream, unsynced. PyIceberg itself only passes buffer_size.

The cost is two fsync calls per written file, and only on a local warehouse. Object stores are not affected. I have not added a property to turn this off. If you would like one, I can add it.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. test_pyarrow_local_fs_syncs_file_and_new_directories_on_close writes through PyArrowFileIO into a path whose parent directories do not exist yet. It then checks that the file and the three directories whose entries changed were synced, by comparing the inodes of the fsynced descriptors.

With the change reverted, the test fails on its assertion (assert [] == [...]: no fsync at all).
tests/io/test_pyarrow.py, tests/avro, tests/catalog/test_sql.py, tests/test_serializers.py and tests/utils/test_manifest.py give the same results with and without the change, apart from the new test.
I also traced the reproduction script from #4145 (create_table plus one append on a SQLite catalog) with strace. On main there is no fsync under the warehouse. With this change, the Parquet file, manifest, manifest list and metadata.json are each synced, together with their directory, before SQLite commits the new metadata_location.

Are there any user-facing changes?
There is no API change. Writes to a local warehouse are now durable once a commit returns, at the cost of the fsync calls above.
title: fix(io): sync local files to disk before the catalog commit

The existing transaction and catalog commit paths provide publication and retry handling. Commit requirements protect ID allocation and concurrent metadata changes.

body:
Closes #4163
Rationale for this change
SqlCatalog.namespace_exists also reports a namespace as existing when a child namespace exists, using LIKE '<namespace>.%'. SQLite evaluates LIKE case-insensitively for ASCII characters, so with only sales.eu in the catalog, namespace_exists("SALES") returned True. As a result create_table("SALES.orders") succeeded in a namespace that does not exist, and create_namespace("SALES") failed with NamespaceAlreadyExistsError. The exact-match comparisons elsewhere in the catalog are case-sensitive, and PostgreSQL's LIKE is case-sensitive too.
This keeps the LIKE filter in the query and re-checks the matched namespace names with a case-sensitive prefix comparison in Python. list_namespaces already filters the same way after its LIKE query. The queries now select only the namespace column with DISTINCT instead of whole rows with LIMIT 1, because a row whose case differs could come back first.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. test_namespace_exists in tests/catalog/test_catalog_behaviors.py now also checks that DB2 and db3.NS1 are not reported as existing when db2.ns1 and db3.ns1.ns2 exist. It fails on main for the memory, sql and sql_without_rowcount catalogs and passes with this change. make test and make lint pass.
Are there any user-facing changes?
On SQLite, namespace_exists and the operations that depend on it no longer treat a namespace as existing just because a child namespace with a different case exists.

body:
Closes #4165
Rationale for this change
_OverwriteFiles._existing_manifests keeps every parent manifest that has no live files. It reads each manifest with discard_deleted=True, so a manifest whose entries are all DELETED comes back empty and takes the "nothing to delete" branch. Each overwrite also writes a manifest for its own deletions, so with explicit delete_data_file overwrites the manifest list grows by one per commit and every later commit and scan opens all of them. In one production table this reached 388 manifests, 387 of them deleted-only.
This skips parent manifests with no added or existing files before reading them, the rule Java applies in MergingSnapshotProducer.apply. Earlier snapshots keep their own manifest lists, so time travel is unaffected, and each new snapshot still lists the manifest recording its own deletions.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. test_overwrite_drops_manifests_without_live_files runs three overwrites and checks that each snapshot lists two manifests and that the first snapshot still reads its own row; on main the counts are [2, 3, 4]. The unit suite and prek pass.
Are there any user-facing changes?
No API change. Tables written with explicit-delete overwrites stop accumulating deleted-only manifests, and existing tables shed them on their next overwrite.
🧑‍💻🤖 — posted via Claude Code

Sourced from filelock's releases.

4.2.1

Bug fixes

On a singleton wrapper, AsyncReadWriteLock.close() and AsyncSoftReadWriteLock.close() end only the holds that tasks acquired through that wrapper. A reader that arrives during close() gets the closed error instead of joining the ending hold. After synchronous code closes or force-releases the shared lock, the wrappers refuse to admit readers into the ended hold, and close() on such a wrapper returns. Closing one wrapper no longer ends a task's nested hold taken through another wrapper on the same path. #832 by @​gaborbernat.
ReadWriteLock locks again after a release() that an exception from a signal handler interrupted. The async read-write wrappers stop admitting readers into such a level. The async read-write locks forget a hold whose backend release failed after the backend let go, and they free the memory of each acquire that times out or is canceled. AsyncFileLock returns from release() after a few hundred acquires gave up behind a waiting one. An exception from a signal handler delivered while an AsyncFileLock call joins its queue no longer blocks every later call on that lock. #833 by @​gaborbernat.
Fix ReadWriteLock acting on -journal, -wal or -shm files another process puts beside its database: a write could land in another file, a reader could get in beside a writer, and an acquire could fail. SQLite now opens the database by name only in a directory no other account can write, and through a private hard link elsewhere. On Windows the directory's access control list decides. Where hard links are unavailable, keep the database in a directory other accounts cannot write, such as one under %LOCALAPPDATA%. The lock removes link directories through a checked descriptor rather than by name, reads a link directory's name only when the locking account owns it, and leaves alone a directory with other content renamed onto a link directory's name. A database whose schema takes more than a few kilobytes to load raises ValueError instead of running past the acquire timeout. #834 by @​gaborbernat.
Fix five bugs in opening the lock file. UnixFileLock no longer truncates a file it did not create, such as one renamed to the lock path, and no longer applies mode to it. An on_acquired hook that writes holder metadata now truncates the file itself. A lease (Linux) or an oplock (Windows) on the lock file or a soft lock's marker no longer holds acquire() past its timeout or blocking=False, and an oplock no longer holds release(); ReadWriteLock on Windows waits for its timeout and raises Timeout. On Windows, a mode without group and other bits, such as 0o600, now creates the lock file with an owner-only permission list; the ReadWriteLock database gets the same. v84.1.0
Features

setuptools.archive_util now raises the new UnsafeMember exception when
an archive member would be extracted outside of the extraction directory,
where previously such a member was silently skipped. Aborting makes a
malicious or malformed archive visible to the caller instead of yielding a
quietly incomplete extraction, and matches the behavior of the standard
library's tarfile extraction filters.

Wheel.install_as_egg no longer creates namespace package directories
outside of the destination egg directory. Entries in a wheel's
namespace_packages.txt were split on . and passed straight to
os.path.join, so an entry that was absolute, drive-qualified, or UNC

the wheel. Namespace entries are now validated as dotted module names on
every platform -- see GHSA-xmj3-9gf7-h52w.

setuptools build backend never reaches it.

requested extraction directory. Both the tar and zip formats specify / as
the only path separator, but the guard against .. components split member
names on / alone, so a name such as ..\escaped.txt was treated as a
single component and then resolved as a traversal by the filesystem on

Release notes
Sourced from graphql-core's releases.

v3.2.12
Patch-release GraphQL-core v3.2.12, based on GraphQL.js v16.14.2.
This patch-release supports Python 3.7 to 3.14.
This is a security release. It fixes two denial-of-service vulnerabilities in the validator and the parser. Upgrading is recommended for all users.
Security fixes:

CVE-2026-75507 (GHSA-vj8h-fx38-h3vc, High) — the OverlappingFieldsCanBeMerged validation rule could be driven into quadratic and worse running time by a small, highly compressible query using repeated inline fragments, occupying a worker for minutes of CPU during validation, before any resolver runs. Validation now enforces a per-document comparison budget and aborts with a GraphQLError once it is exhausted.
CVE-2026-75508 (GHSA-r77w-qph3-7vf8, High) — comment tokens were allocated and retained but not counted toward the parser's max_tokens limit, so a comment-padded document could bypass the limit while allocating one token object per comment. max_tokens now counts every token the parser consumes, including skipped comments.

Please note the two behaviour changes this implies:

A pathological query that previously validated — slowly — now produces a validation error. Realistic queries stay far below the limit, which defaults to 250,000 field comparisons and can be adjusted by assigning to graphql.validation.rules.overlapping_fields_can_be_merged.MAX_FIELD_COMPARISONS.
Comments now count toward max_tokens, so a comment-heavy document that was previously accepted may now be rejected. If you parse documents with substantial comments and set max_tokens, you may need to raise the limit. The token_count of a parsed document now includes comments as well.

Both limits complement, but do not replace, a request body-size limit applied to the decompressed request body in your web framework.
Other changes:

Updated development dependencies and CI tooling.

The security issues were reported by @​BZHunt, who also reviewed the fixes before release. In memory of ZaX, who was the driving force behind this discovery. The first one was also independently found and diagnosed by @​bcmyguest.

body:
Closes #2604
Rationale for this change
expire_snapshots only rewrites the table metadata, so files that only expired snapshots referenced stay on the file system. Trino and Spark both clean those up.
This adds an opt-in clean_expired_files() step, following the approach agreed in the issue: after the expiration has committed, compare the expired snapshots against the snapshots left in the table and delete the difference, without listing the object store. ʕ•ᴥ•ʔ
How files are chosen
Similar to Iceberg Java's ReachableFileCleanup, but more conservative:

Candidates: entries (including DELETED entries) of manifests used by the expired snapshots and by no snapshot left in the table.
Subtract: if there are candidates, read the live entries of every manifest left in the table and remove their paths.
Abort on read failure: if any manifest list or manifest cannot be read, nothing is deleted.

Read cost:

When snapshots are selected, the manifest lists of the expired and the remaining snapshots are read.
A table written only with fast appends reads no manifests, because no manifest goes away.
Reads run in parallel on the shared executor, and only file paths are kept in memory.

Concurrent ref changes
Without a check, the catalog would drop a branch or tag that another writer created on a snapshot being expired, and the cleanup would delete files that ref still needs. So commit() reloads the latest table metadata first:

Change by another writer
Result

Before the reload: a branch or tag points at a selected snapshot
ValueError, nothing is expired

After the reload: a branch or tag other than main is moved or removed
commit fails (AssertRefSnapshotId), nothing is deleted

After the reload: an append to main
expiration succeeds (main is not asserted)

After the reload: a new branch or tag on a selected snapshot, or main reset to one
not detected: the catalog drops that ref with the snapshot, and its files are deleted

gc.enabled differs from Java
Java rejects any expiration when gc.enabled is false, because its expiration deletes files by default. Here, expiring without clean_expired_files() only changes the metadata, so it stays allowed; only clean_expired_files() raises a ValueError. This matches the consensus in the issue that deleting files is opt-in. The value is read from the latest table metadata.
Are these changes tested?
Yes, in tests/table/test_expire_snapshots.py:

Default: no call, or enabled=False after enabling, deletes nothing.
Deleted vs kept: see the table under user-facing changes, including files still used by retained snapshots, tags, or snapshots another writer committed.
Read cost: a shared manifest is read once and only for live entries; a fast-append history reads no manifests.
Concurrent refs: every row of the table above except the undetected one, including a table object refreshed after the selection.
Failures: commit failure deletes nothing; a failed delete is skipped and logged; a corrupt retained manifest stops the cleanup while the expiration stays committed; autocommit and gc.enabled checks.

Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes. ExpireSnapshots gets a new clean_expired_files(enabled: bool = True) method:
table.maintenance.expire_snapshots().clean_expired_files().older_than(cutoff).commit()
After the expiration has committed:

Deleted
Kept

Data and delete files of the expired snapshots that no remaining snapshot references as live
Files any remaining snapshot references as live

Manifests and manifest lists of the expired snapshots that no remaining snapshot uses
Previous metadata files

Statistics and partition statistics files of the expired snapshots
Statistics and partition statistics files the metadata after the commit still references

Orphan files no snapshot ever referenced

On failure:

A file whose deletion raises an OSError is skipped and a warning is logged.
A manifest list or manifest that cannot be read: no files are deleted.
Any other exception: files not deleted yet are kept.

body:
Closes #4190
Rationale for this change
UpdateSchema._commit only sent AssertCurrentSchemaId, so a stale update_schema could commit after another writer had moved the current schema away and back. For example:

writer A adds a column (field id 2, schema 1), then drops it, which makes schema 0 current again
writer B, loaded before A's changes, adds a column: its AssertCurrentSchemaId(0) still passes, so it reuses field id 2 and adds a second schema with id 1

Java's UpdateRequirements adds AssertLastAssignedFieldId(base.lastColumnId()) when a commit adds a schema (update(MetadataUpdate.AddSchema)). pyiceberg already defines AssertLastAssignedFieldId but never sent it.
What changed

UpdateSchema._commit adds AssertLastAssignedFieldId with the transaction's last_column_id when it adds a new schema
this follows UpdateSpec._commit, which adds AssertLastAssignedPartitionId when it adds a spec
switching back to an existing schema adds no schema, so it only sends AssertCurrentSchemaId, as before

With this change, writer B fails with CommitFailedException and the table stays unchanged (｀・ω・´)
Are these changes tested?
Yes. test_concurrent_add_column_after_add_and_drop in tests/catalog/test_catalog_behaviors.py runs the scenario from the issue against the memory and SQL catalogs:

with this change, writer B fails with last assigned field id has changed: expected 3, found 4
without it, the test fails with DID NOT RAISE CommitFailedException

Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes, a bug fix: a stale update_schema that adds a schema now raises CommitFailedException when the table's last assigned field id has changed, instead of reusing field ids. Refresh the table and retry, as with other requirement failures (・ω・)b

body:
Closes #4193
Rationale for this change
Applying RemoveSnapshotsUpdate set parent_snapshot_id to None on every snapshot whose parent was removed. Since #3512, an incremental append scan accepts an expired exclusive start if some ancestor of the end snapshot still has it as its parent, so this reset makes that case fail after expire_snapshots. For example:

append three times, then expire the first snapshot with expire_snapshots().by_id(...)
incremental_append_scan(from_snapshot_id_exclusive=<first snapshot id>) raises Starting snapshot (exclusive) ... is not a parent ancestor of end snapshot ... instead of returning the rows of the second and third appends

The reset came in with #1561; it was not discussed in review there, and the Java code linked in that review keeps the parent.
Java keeps the parent id: TableMetadata.Builder.rewriteSnapshotsInternal only drops the removed snapshots from the list and leaves the remaining ones unchanged. The spec does not ask for the parent to still exist either; the field description of parent-snapshot-id only says "Omitted for any snapshot with no parent".
What changed

the RemoveSnapshotsUpdate handler in pyiceberg/table/update/__init__.py drops the removed snapshots and keeps the remaining ones as they are
a dangling parent id is already handled by ancestors_of, which stops when snapshot_by_id returns None, the same way as Java's SnapshotUtil.ancestorsOf

The scan from the example now returns the rows of the second and third appends (｀・ω・´)
Are these changes tested?
Yes, in tests/table/test_init.py:

test_incremental_append_scan_from_snapshot_expired_by_maintenance runs the example against the memory and SQL catalogs and checks that the scan returns [20, 30]. Without this change, the scan raises the ValueError above
test_update_remove_snapshots asserted the old behavior (parent_snapshot_id is None). It now asserts that the remaining snapshot keeps its parent id from the fixture, and fails without this change with assert None == 3051729675574597004

Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes, a bug fix: after RemoveSnapshotsUpdate is applied in pyiceberg, for example by expire_snapshots, the remaining snapshots keep their parent_snapshot_id, even if that snapshot no longer exists in the metadata. This applies to catalogs that apply the update in pyiceberg, such as SQL, Glue and Hive; for REST catalogs, the server applies it. Parent ids that were already cleared before this fix are not restored. Code that read parent_snapshot_id is None to find the oldest remaining snapshot should check whether snapshot_by_id returns None instead (・ω・)b
AI Disclosure
Human-led contribution. Grok Bot, working for dragonknightk, assisted with this change. All submitted content was reviewed by a human before submission.
title: Keep the parent snapshot id when removing snapshots

body:
What
This change replaces Makefile and .pre-commit-config.yaml with a single noxfile.py, and leaves the justfile as a thin entry point with one command line per recipe. CI now calls the same nox sessions that a developer runs locally, so there is one place to look when a check fails.

noxfile.py defines 24 sessions, six of which form the gate while the rest are test suites and local actions
justfile holds no logic and is 141 lines long
Tool versions live in pyproject.toml and uv.lock only, so each session installs the dependency group it needs by name
The Python matrix comes from the trove classifiers in pyproject.toml rather than from a workflow matrix
Every workflow calls the nox sessions directly, and the justfile stays a convenience for local runs

This is not the shortest way to write this file, because I copied the old behaviour first. The pre-commit hooks let pre-commit choose the files to check, which nox does not do, so noxfile.py carries helpers that walk the tree, read .gitignore, and separate text files from binary ones. This will be cleaned in up in a future commit.
Also, I've had added new dependencies groups into the project so that nox sessions install only what they need, this makes the sessions faster and less prone to weird bugs.
Why
This is an effort to modernize/centralize dev tooling, reduce version drift, and make the project easier to reason about/improve the dev experience. Currently three files describe the same checks in three different ways and contain some logic in them, so learning what CI runs meant opening the Makefile, then .pre-commit-config.yaml, and then the workflow.
Pre-commit adds another YAML-based configuration layer instead of respecting pyproject.toml, and the maintainers have explicitly declined to support pyproject.toml configuration . That leaves hook definitions, versions, and additional dependencies outside the dependency configuration used by the rest of the project, which causes version drift. In addition, commands were sometimes nested: CI ran make lint which ran prek run -a, which ran a hook, which ran a tool in an environment that pre-commit had built, etc. This introduces many opportunities for misalignment between local and CI results.
The mypy hook is a concrete example. Its isolated environment and pre-commit's tracked-file selection do not match a direct mypy cli run from the development environment, so for example a passing hook cannot serve as an apples to apples baseline for comparing a potential mypy with ty migration.
With this PR, the logic exists in one place, in Python, and reads native dependencies, so a version bump touches pyproject.toml and uv.lock and nothing else. CI and local development invoke the same nox sessions with the same files and dependencies

Closes #4202
Rationale for this change
UpdateSortOrder only asserts the default sort order id, so a stale handle can commit an AddSortOrderUpdate whose id already exists. When the orders are equal, the metadata ends up with two sort orders sharing an id, which Java's TableMetadataParser rejects. When they differ, it raises a non-retryable ValueError.
This mirrors Java's TableMetadata.Builder.addSortOrder:

Reuse the id of an existing sort order with the same fields instead of appending a duplicate.
Assign the next free id when the requested id is taken by a different sort order.
Track the last added sort order in the update context so SetDefaultSortOrderUpdate(-1) resolves to it, rather than the highest id.

Are these changes tested?
Yes. New catalog behavior tests cover the stale-handle scenarios from the issue and multiple sort order changes in one transaction. There are also unit tests for update_table_metadata.
Are there any user-facing changes?
No API changes. Stale sort order updates no longer produce invalid metadata.

body:
Closes #4203
Rationale for this change
_task_to_record_batches re-bound the row filter to each data file's own schema, which converted the literal to the file's older type. After update_column("f", DoubleType()) on a float column, 0.1 became the 32-bit 0.1, so f > 0.1 and f != 0.1 dropped rows written before the promotion even though the scan returns them as 0.10000000149011612. A widened decimal (decimal(5,2) to decimal(12,2)) raised ArrowInvalid for the same reason.
The filter now stays bound to the table schema and Arrow compares the mixed types. This matches delete(), upsert and the stats-based file pruning, which already compare in the table's type. Previously scan and delete disagreed on which rows matched.
What changed

Added resolve_missing_columns, which replaces predicates on columns missing from the file with constants (projected partition value, then initial-default, as before) and leaves the other predicates bound to the table schema. It shares its logic with _ColumnNameTranslator, and translate_column_names is unchanged.
_task_to_record_batches uses it and passes file_schema to expression_to_pyarrow, which resolves column names by field ID.

Not in this PR
IN / NOT IN on a promoted float still compares in the file's type, because Arrow casts the isin value set to the column type. That is unchanged from before and can be a follow-up.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. New tests cover float to double, decimal widening and int to long. They also cover nested, renamed and later-added columns, files from before and after the promotion in one scan, nulls, positional deletes, partition-projected and initial-default columns, and delete() matching scan. This does not change which snapshots are retained or their explicit snapshot-ID lookup. It does not reconstruct history already damaged by earlier expirations.

body:
Closes #4195
Rationale for this change
Writing to a branch that does not exist creates it, but the new snapshot gets no parent, so the branch starts empty instead of from the state of the table.
tbl.append(pa.table({"x": [1, 2]}))
tbl.append(pa.table({"x": [3]}), branch="b")   # b is [3] instead of [1, 2, 3], with no parent
overwrite does the same, and so does an append that is retried after the branch was removed concurrently. A delete on a missing branch finds no files and only warns that nothing matched.
Java starts from main. SnapshotProducer.apply() takes the parent from SnapshotUtil.latestSnapshot(base, targetBranch), which returns metadata.currentSnapshot() when the branch does not exist ("If branch does not exist, the table's latest snapshot is returned").
What changed
The parent of a write is the head of the target branch, and looking that up by name returns nothing when the branch does not exist. Five places depend on that lookup:

Where
Now

_SnapshotProducer._current_branch_head_id
Falls back to the current snapshot. Sets the parent for append, overwrite and delete, on the first attempt and on a retry

_OverwriteFiles._existing_manifests
Reads the manifests of that parent instead of looking up the branch again, so the files that are not rewritten are kept

UpdateSnapshot.overwrite
Uses the OVERWRITE operation when the branch does not exist but the table has a current snapshot, since the rewrite removes data files

Transaction.delete
Scans the branch if it exists, and main otherwise, the same way upsert already does

CommitWindow.resolve
Uses the same fallback for the end of the validation window, so a retried delete or overwrite validates the snapshots added to main since it started

Left out

A table without snapshots: writing to a missing branch still raises CommitFailedException: Requirement failed: Table has no snapshots and can only be written to the main BRANCH., since the parent is still None there (・ω・)b
A table written concurrently: writing to a missing branch raises the existing ValueError: Cannot add snapshot with sequence number 2 older than last sequence number 2, and that attempt is not retried. The same happens when the branch exists, so it is left out of this PR

Are these changes tested?
Yes, against the memory and SQL catalogs:

Test
Checks

test_append_to_missing_branch_starts_from_main (tests/catalog/test_catalog_behaviors.py)
The example above: b is [1, 2, 3], and its parent is the snapshot of main

body:
Closes #4197
Rationale for this change
A scan whose snapshot_id names no snapshot, for example an expired one, answers two ways: plan_files() returns no tasks and count() returns 0, while to_arrow() on the same scan raises ValueError: Snapshot not found: <id>.
Reproducer:

append twice, then expire the first snapshot with t.maintenance.expire_snapshots().by_id(s1).commit()
t.scan(snapshot_id=s1).count() returns 0 and plan_files() returns []
t.scan(snapshot_id=s1).to_arrow() raises ValueError: Snapshot not found: ...

The local planning path returned [] whenever self.snapshot() was None, which covers both an empty table and an id that is not in the metadata. Only the empty table should plan to nothing.
Java makes the same distinction. SnapshotScan.useSnapshot rejects an unknown id with Preconditions.checkArgument(table().snapshot(scanSnapshotId) != null, "Cannot find snapshot with ID %s", scanSnapshotId), so the snapshot == null branch in SnapshotScan.planFiles() only returns an empty result for an empty table.
What changed

Where
Now

DataScan._plan_files_local
Raises ValueError(f"Snapshot not found: {self.snapshot_id}") when a snapshot_id is set but not found, the same error that projection() and therefore to_arrow() already raise

count()
Uses plan_files(), so it raises as well

to_arrow(), to_arrow_batch_reader()
Already raised from projection(), unchanged

A scan without a snapshot_id on a table without snapshots
Still plans to nothing

Why planning, not the scan constructor
Java checks when the snapshot is set on the scan; this change checks when the files are planned. pyiceberg accepts the id in the DataScan constructor and in update(), and TableScan.snapshot() returns None for an unknown id, which test_table_scan_missing_snapshot_zero relies on. Checking in planning keeps those as they are and raises at the same point as to_arrow(), which only fails once it is called.
Server-side planning
Unchanged: the snapshot id is sent to the REST server, which plans against its own metadata. The Java reference implementation calls useSnapshot in CatalogHandlers.planTableScan, so it rejects an unknown id with a 400 that pyiceberg raises as BadRequestError. With server-side planning, plan_files() and count() therefore raise the server's error when the server rejects the id, instead of the ValueError that to_arrow() raises from projection() before planning (・ω・)b
Are these changes tested?
Yes, in tests/table/test_init.py:

Test
Checks

test_table_scan_plan_files_missing_snapshot
plan_files() and count() raise Snapshot not found: 0 for a scan of table_v2 with snapshot id 0, which the fixture does not have. The id 0 also makes sure the check does not treat the id as a boolean. Without this change, the test fails with DID NOT RAISE ValueError

test_data_scan_plan_files_no_current_snapshot
A table without snapshots is already covered: plan_files() returns [] and count() returns 0 for a scan without a snapshot_id of a table without snapshots

Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes, a bug fix: plan_files() and count() on a scan whose snapshot_id names no snapshot now raise ValueError: Snapshot not found: <id>, instead of returning no tasks and 0 (｀・ω・´)

body:
Closes #4184
Rationale for this change
When delete() (and overwrite() with an overwrite_filter) has to rewrite a data file, it keeps the rows that _expression_to_complementary_pyarrow selects. That filter was NOT f, OR'd with c IS NULL for every column c that f reads without a null check. Under pyarrow's three-valued logic that goes wrong both ways when a column is null:

NOT f is null where f is null, so the row is dropped even though f did not match it: x=2 in the issue (p == 2, v null) is deleted by (p == 1 AND v IS NULL) OR (p == 2 AND v == 'c').
c IS NULL keeps a row whenever c is null, even where f is still true: p == 1 OR v == 'c' keeps x=1 (p == 1, v null).

A row should be deleted exactly where f is true, which are the rows scan(row_filter=f) returns. The complement is now NOT coalesce(f, false). The NaN handling (OR is_nan(c) for columns the filter does not NaN-check) is left as it was.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. test_delete_and_overwrite_filter_with_null in tests/catalog/test_catalog_behaviors.py runs the issue's two filters plus v != 'c' and NOT (v == 'c') through delete() and overwrite() on every local catalog, and checks that the rows left are the ones scan(row_filter=...) does not return. It fails on main and passes with this change. test_expression_to_complementary_pyarrow is updated for the new expression. Unit tests in tests/io, tests/table, tests/catalog and tests/expressions: 2658 passed (the only failures are the four Kerberos tests in test_hive.py, which need the hive-kerberos extra I did not install). ruff check and ruff format --check are clean.
Are there any user-facing changes?
delete() and overwrite(..., overwrite_filter=...) no longer delete rows the filter does not match, or keep rows it does, when a column the filter reads is null.
title: Keep rows where a delete filter evaluates to null

body:
Closes #4182
Rationale for this change
expire_snapshots().older_than(dt) converts the cutoff with datetime_to_millis, which reads a naive datetime as UTC. The docs call it as older_than(datetime.now() - timedelta(days=3)), and datetime.now() is a naive local time, so east of UTC the cutoff lands later than asked (in Tokyo, datetime.now() - timedelta(hours=1) expires snapshots that are seconds old) and west of UTC it lands earlier.
older_than() now reads a naive datetime as local time, as datetime.timestamp() does, by calling astimezone() on it before the conversion. An aware datetime is handled as before. datetime_to_millis itself is unchanged, since a naive value there means UTC for timestamp columns.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. test_expire_snapshots_older_than_reads_naive_datetime_as_local_time in tests/table/test_expire_snapshots.py sets TZ to Asia/Tokyo and checks that a naive cutoff one minute before a snapshot keeps it and one minute after expires it. It fails on main and passes with this change (it is skipped where time.tzset is unavailable). The issue's script now keeps all three snapshots under Asia/Tokyo, America/Los_Angeles and UTC. tests/table and tests/utils: 768 passed. ruff check and ruff format --check are clean.
Are there any user-facing changes?
older_than() with a naive datetime now uses the local time zone instead of UTC. Callers who passed naive UTC datetimes on purpose should pass an aware one (datetime.now(timezone.utc)).
title: Read a naive datetime in older_than as local time

body:
Closes #4192
Rationale for this change
Transaction.dynamic_partition_overwrite wrote its data files using the
committed table metadata, but built its delete filter from the transaction's
metadata. After an update_spec in the same transaction, the two disagree on
the partition spec, so the wrong rows can be deleted and new files recorded
under the wrong partition. After an in-transaction add_column, it raises
ValueError instead.
This passes self.table_metadata to _dataframe_to_data_files, matching
append, overwrite and delete.
Are these changes tested?
Yes. Two new tests cover update_spec and add_column inside a transaction.
Both fail without the fix and pass with it. The full unit suite, the Docker
integration suite and the lint hooks pass locally.
Are there any user-facing changes?
Yes, only as the bug fix: both cases now behave correctly.
title: Use transaction metadata in dynamic_partition_overwrite
